source.title: Large System Analysis of Box-Relaxation in Correlated Massive MIMO Systems Under Imperfect CSI (Extended Version)

record.tranche_reason: The study reports a double-descent-shaped result for the LS detector and says the BRO box constraint mitigates it. This refines the general claim in a MIMO-decoding setting.
record.gate_note: The study's own Figure 6 and accompanying text report MSE and BER trends over the receive-to-transmit antenna ratio. Results cited from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: A new setting (MIMO detection) where the study's own simulations in Fig. 6 show a double-descent curve for the least-squares/zero-forcing decoder. Its MSE and BER are plotted against β = m/n, the ratio of measurements (receive antennas) to unknowns (transmit antennas). This is the linear least-squares analogue of a sample-wise or overparameterization-ratio sweep. It does not reproduce either original's method, so it is not T1 or T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The author concludes that the BRO decoder outperforms LS/ZF and mitigates the double-descent effect seen with conventional decoders such as ZF. The author also says this is expected, viewing the box constraint as an ℓ∞ regularizer. The paper's main contributions, though, are asymptotic MSE/BER formulas and optimal pilot/data power allocation, not double descent.
record.recipe_differences: This is a large-system analysis and simulation of MIMO decoders under imperfect CSI and channel correlation, with sweeps over antenna ratio; it does not reproduce the original studies' model-size, epoch, or sample-size experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Decoder choice: the authors report double descent for LS/ZF and mitigation by the BRO box constraint.

fits_no_version.finding: A fixed ℓ∞ box constraint, which the authors call a regularizer, reduces the LS double-descent peak in MSE and BER.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Constraints that act as fixed (untuned) regularizers dampen the interpolation peak, not only optimally tuned ridge.

record.problems: Figure 6 provides the plotted values without numerical results in the text. The reported sweep is in antenna ratio, not model capacity, and only one setting is described for Figure 6.

untested.parts: All: no deep networks and no model-size sweep.
Learned predictors on held-out data. Here the error is signal-recovery error in a linear inverse problem, not the test error of a trained model.
Capacity is varied only through the ratio m/n over about 0.4–2. No growth of model capacity at fixed data, and no other model classes.

No label-noise manipulation, no multiple peaks, and no optimally tuned regularization. The box constraint is a fixed, untuned ℓ∞ constraint, and the authors' link to regularization is their interpretation.
All: no recounting of effective parameters.

record.verdict_notes: Double descent is a side observation in one figure (Fig. 6), described qualitatively with no numbers, no uncertainty and a single setting. The paper is single-author. Theory assumes β > 1/2, so the low-β side of the LS curve rests on simulation only. The text does not state how LS is computed when β < 1 (for example, minimum-norm). The sweep axis is better read as samples per parameter (V3) than as model capacity, which is why V3 links were added. The record's T5 tranche is changed to T3: the study reports a new-setting result rather than arguing that a version is wrong. The record's peer_reviewed field gives a venue (GC Wkshps) that the text does not state.

versions.untested_parts: Deep-network test error versus model size.
Changing training sample size near an interpolation threshold.
The study varies antenna ratio in MIMO decoders, not model capacity in a learning model class.
A single effective-complexity measure predicting peak location across axes.
Effects of label noise or variance, multiple peaks, and disappearance under optimally tuned regularization.
Recounting complexity by effective parameter number to test whether the second descent becomes an ordinary U-shaped curve.
